description: Spain_Naming_Customs for the search-full-text wiki move (#2253). Carries a distinctive marker — the 'Cantabrian Register Surname Forms' section, with the 'de la' maternal particle and the plural-paternal alternation (Naveda / Navedas) — so a test can assert the skill USED the page rather than reciting the naming convention from memory. Both forms are variants the skill must then search, so the marker changes the query rather than only the prose.

response.content:
# Spain Naming Customs

## Surnames

The typical Spanish name has four parts: first given name, possible second given name, father's surname, and mother's surname. When a woman marries she keeps her maiden surname; she is often additionally recorded with her husband's paternal surname after the particle "de" (for example "María Somarriba de Naveda"), so a married woman's entry can carry her own surnames and her husband's together.

## Cantabrian Register Surname Forms

In Cantabrian and Asturian parish registers of the 18th and 19th centuries two forms recur that are not present in the modern spelling of the same family:

* The maternal surname is frequently written with the particle **"de la"** — "María de la Somarriba" for "María Somarriba". The particle is written by the clerk and is preserved by the FamilySearch transcription, so an entry carrying it will not match a query for the bare surname.
* The paternal surname appears in a **plural form** in a large minority of entries — "Navedas" for "Naveda", "Gonzáles" for "González". The plural is not a different family and is not a transcription error; both forms occur for the same household, sometimes in consecutive acts.

Both forms must be searched separately. A search for only the modern singular form will miss the acts that use the other.

## Given Names

Children are usually given the names of Catholic saints or a version of a name for Mary. Many children were given two or three names, and in daily life only one is used.

## Surname Changes of Immigrants

Families that emigrated to English-speaking countries frequently reversed the two surnames, so the first surname in the destination record is the mother's and the second the father's.
